To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exposure to emotionally aversively valenced pictures did not differentially affect resting‐state measures in healthy young adults.

the short‐term effect, as measured in the resting state, of exposure to emotional stimuli is negligible in healthy young adults, and that the effect of negative valency on memory performance is observable.
resting‐state networks and the amygdala’s low frequency fluctuations appear to be unaffected in healthy young adults by preceding exposure to negative emotional pictures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether exposure to emotional pictures affects subsequent brain resting‐state networks in a way that can be observed in the absence of the emotional pictures.
the question of whether the brain’s resting‐state functional connectivity is altered by preceding exposure to emotionally averse visual stimuli.
the short‐term effect on resting‐state networks of emotionally aversive pictures in healthy young adults.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in healthy young adults, the confrontation with emotional pictures does not affect resting‐state measures.
, in the context of this study, the amygdala is not involved in the short‐term effect on resting‐state connectivity.
the short‐term effects of emotional stimuli on subsequent resting‐state functional connectivity remain elusive.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the short‐term effect on the amygdala and the hippocampus, as well as on resting‐state networks, is not detectable in a healthy young sample.
, in healthy young adults, exposure to emotional pictures does not affect the temporal unfolding of resting‐state networks.
exposure to emotional pictures, in this case negative ones, does not affect the resting‐state networks in healthy young adults, as demonstrated in the present study.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the amygdala, which is the brain structure most strongly involved in the processing of emotionally salient stimuli, does not appear to be affected by preceding exposure to emotionally salient stimuli.

resting‐state networks appear to be resilient to the immediate emotional impact of stimuli, which is in line with the notion that the brain is capable of returning to a resting‐state baseline after the presentation of emotional stimuli.
the short‐term effect on resting‐state networks and amygdala connectivity of emotional stimuli in healthy young adult subjects does not differ from the effect of neutral stimuli.
